items.stem: Explain why the war on the Western Front became a stalemate.

items.stem: Explain whether you agree that war memorials tell us more about the people who built them than about the wars they remember. Give one reason for and one reason against.
items.answer: Agree: Their words, symbols and choice of names reflect the values of their time (e.g. “glorious sacrifice” in 1920s Britain). Later memorials such as the Berlin Holocaust memorial (2005) reflect modern concerns. Disagree: Lists of names give valuable evidence of the scale of loss in each community. They record dates, battles and units. Judgement: They tell us about both, but are most valuable as evidence of how societies chose to remember.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1 mark): one simple reason. Level 2 (2-3 marks): one explained reason for AND one against, with accurate detail.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “Treaty of Versailles”?
options: An international organisation set up in 1920 to keep peace through cooperation and collective security.
The peace treaty between the Allies and Germany signed on 28 June 1919.
A ruler with total power who is not limited by laws, elections or a parliament.
The policy of giving in to some of a dictator’s demands in order to avoid war.

items.stem: Explain why the Treaty of Versailles caused resentment in Germany.
items.answer: Germans had not been allowed to negotiate (a diktat); Article 231 blamed Germany for the war; reparations damaged the economy; Germany lost about 13% of its land, all its colonies and was disarmed, which felt humiliating.

items.stem: Explain how Nazi persecution of Jews increased between 1933 and 1945.
items.answer: From boycotts of Jewish shops (1933) and the Nuremberg Laws (1935) removing citizenship, to violence on Kristallnacht (1938), ghettos in occupied Poland, mass shootings by the Einsatzgruppen (from 1941) and death camps such as Auschwitz after the Wannsee Conference (1942).

items.stem: Study Source D, the diary of a Jewish teenager hiding in Amsterdam, 1943 (adapted). “We hear that our Jewish friends are being taken away in groups. The Gestapo treat them roughly and transport them in cattle trucks to the camps in the east. We must keep very quiet here.” (a) What can you infer from Source D about the persecution of Jews in occupied Europe? (b) Use your own knowledge to describe one aspect of the persecution of Jews in occupied Europe that Source D does not show.
items.answer: (a) Jews in occupied countries lived in fear as they were rounded up and deported to camps; some went into hiding. (b) What happened in the camps, or the scale of the Holocaust across Europe.

items.stem: Sequence these events from earliest to latest. A: The Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe opened in Berlin. B: India Gate, the All India War Memorial in New Delhi, was inaugurated. C: The Hiroshima Peace Memorial (Genbaku Dome) became a UNESCO World Heritage Site. D: The Thiepval Memorial to the Missing of the Somme was unveiled.

items.stem: Source D is taken from the inscription on a village war memorial in England, unveiled in 1921 (adapted). It says: “To the glorious memory of the men of this parish who gave their lives for King and Country, 1914-1918. Their name liveth for evermore.” Use it to answer the questions. (a) What can you infer from Source D about how communities remembered the First World War in the 1920s? (b) Explain one reason why Source D may be reliable and one reason why it may not be reliable.
items.answer: (a) Communities in the 1920s remembered the dead as heroes who sacrificed themselves for a noble cause. (b) May be reliable: it shows the attitudes of the community at the time the memorial was built. May not be reliable: it presents an official, positive view and hides the horror or doubts some survivors felt.

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “competition between powers to gain and control colonies and empires”.
items.answer: Imperialism
items.markingKey: Imperialism: competition between powers to gain and control colonies and empires. [1]

items.stem: Explain how the naval race increased tension between Britain and Germany.
items.answer: Germany’s build-up of a large navy threatened British naval supremacy, which Britain relied on to protect its empire and trade; the race to build dreadnoughts created fear and suspicion and pushed Britain closer to France and Russia.
items.markingKey: 1 mark threat; 1 mark fear/suspicion; 1 mark effect on alliances [3]

items.stem: A student investigating who was to blame for the First World War finds Source D. Source D: a historian writing in 2013 about the outbreak of war. “The statesmen of 1914 were like sleepwalkers: watchful but unseeing. Each took decisions that made sense to them, yet together they led Europe into catastrophe.” What can you infer from Source D about responsibility for the war?
items.answer: The historian argues that many leaders, not one country, shared responsibility for the war.
items.markingKey: 1 mark valid inference; 1 mark supported with a detail from the source [2]

items.stem: Explain why the British government used propaganda during the First World War.
items.answer: To encourage men to volunteer (before conscription), keep up morale, encourage saving food and money, and create hatred of the enemy so people would support the war.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “reparations”?
options: Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles, which made Germany accept blame for the war.
A nationalist, anti-democratic political system with a single party and an all-powerful leader, first in Mussolini’s Italy.
A ruler with total power who is not limited by laws, elections or a parliament.
Payments for war damage that Germany was made to pay to the Allies.
items.answer: Payments for war damage that Germany was made to pay to the Allies.
items.markingKey: Reparations: payments for war damage that Germany was made to pay to the Allies. [1]

items.stem: Explain why the League of Nations failed to keep peace in the 1930s.
items.answer: The USA never joined and Germany, Japan and Italy left; it had no army of its own; sanctions were weak and slow; it failed to stop Japan in Manchuria (1931) and Italy in Abyssinia (1935-36), so aggressors saw it could be ignored.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each explained weakness or example up to [3]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “The Soviet Union suffered the greatest number of deaths of any country in the Second World War.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Estimates are around 24-27 million Soviet deaths, military and civilian.

items.stem: Explain two ways the Second World War affected civilians in Britain.
items.answer: Bombing in the Blitz killed about 43 000 and destroyed homes; evacuation separated families; rationing from January 1940 limited food and clothes; women were conscripted for war work from 1941.
items.markingKey: 2 marks each explained effect [4]

items.stem: Estimated deaths in the Second World War (millions, military then civilian): Soviet Union 8.7 and 17; Poland 0.2 and 5.6; Japan 2.1 and 0.6; USA 0.41 and 0.01; United Kingdom 0.38 and 0.07. Estimates vary between historians. (a) Explain why estimates of deaths in the Second World War vary. (b) Compare the experience of civilians in the United Kingdom with those in the Soviet Union, using the data.
items.answer: (a) Records were destroyed or never kept, especially in occupied areas; borders changed; deaths from famine and disease are hard to count; governments sometimes changed figures for political reasons. (b) UK civilian deaths (about 0.07 million, mainly from bombing) were tiny compared with the Soviet Union (about 17 million) because the USSR was invaded and occupied, with sieges, massacres and famine.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each reason [2] (b) 1 mark comparison with figures; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: A class is investigating the significance of the first day of the Battle of the Somme (1916). One student uses these criteria: how many people were affected, how far it caused change, and whether it is still remembered today. Explain why people in different countries might judge the significance of this event differently.
items.answer: National experiences differ: a victory for one side is a defeat for another; some countries lost far more people; memory is shaped by national identity.
